description: AnaLog is a solo team. I'm Ana, a Computer Science Engineering student and English teacher who loves space, weather and turning data into clear, beautiful tools. This weekend I'm building an interactive web app that helps people explore Earth's analogs of Mars and the Moon, using NASA open data. Skills I bring: web development, data visualization, design and science communication. Solo team, but always happy to connect with fellow space and data fans.
summary: Analog Window is a web app that searches the whole Earth for places that behave most like Mars or the Moon's south pole, and finds the month when each place matches best. It scores 1,567 land points with 20 years of NASA climate data, ranks the strongest "twins", and turns them into a field test plan: one place and month for each mission phase, which a team can edit and download as a PDF. Every site also lists what it cannot reproduce, because no place on Earth has low gravity, a vacuum or Martian radiation. It matters because analog testing is how missions like Artemis are prepared, and most teams still go back to the same few famous sites.
details:
What it does. Analog Window answers three questions for anyone preparing a Mars or Moon mission on Earth:

  • Where: which places on Earth match Mars or the Moon's south pole most closely, found by a systematic search instead of a list of known sites.
  • When: the month each place matches best. The same place can be a strong twin in September and a weak one in January, so the app shows a best window for every place.
  • What not: what no place on Earth can copy, so a team knows what each test is and isn't valid for.

How it works.

  1. A 4° grid covers all of Earth's land (1,287 points), plus a finer 1° grid in the four strongest regions (Puna/Altiplano, Qaidam, Tibet/Changtang and Pamir) and 8 well-known analog sites as benchmarks.
  2. For every point and month, the app takes 20-year monthly averages (2001–2020) from the NASA POWER Climatology API: temperature, daily range, rain, humidity, air pressure, wind, sunlight, clear-sky share and UV.
  3. No place on Earth reaches Mars or Moon values, so each factor is scored as a percentile: how far a place goes in the target's direction compared with the rest of Earth's land (drier, colder, thinner air, more UV, bigger temperature swings, clearer skies).
  4. A mission profile (Balanced, Mobility & robotics, Construction & habitat, Resources, Life detection, Human operations) sets the weights, and the user can fine-tune them with sliders. The weighted average is the twin score.
  5. The field test plan picks the best place and month for each mission phase, one per month and far enough apart to test different conditions. Phases can be skipped and places swapped, and the plan exports as a one-page PDF brief.
  6. For the candidate sites, the surface was checked in NASA Worldview imagery, and each one lists what to test there and what it is not valid for.

Validation. Known analogs were scored the same way, as a test of the method. Dry desert analogs such as the Atacama, Death Valley and the Mars Desert Research Station rank in the top ~22% of Earth's land. The Qaidam Basin, an established Mars analog region, was found by the search on its own. Sites famous for their geology, like Haughton Crater or Iceland's lava fields, score low, because the score measures climate, not landforms. The app says this openly.

What's new(creativity): The strongest Mars twins it finds include less-studied high plateaus, such as the High Puna salt plateau in the Andes (best in September) and highland areas of Tibet, next to the classic sites. Adding time to the search (the best window) and turning the results into a ready plan are the main differences from a static map of analogs.

Intended impact. Analog Window helps mission teams choose test sites by data instead of habit, plan a whole year of field tests in minutes, and avoid tests that Earth cannot make valid. It also makes Mars and Moon preparation understandable for students and the public, using free NASA data that anyone can check. Most analog tools compare how a place looks; Analog Window compares how it behaves, and when. Conditions are scored automatically for all of Earth’s land; terrain is checked in NASA Worldview imagery for the strongest candidates.

Who it's for: Engineers planning rover, habitat or operations tests; scientists choosing field sites; and students or the public who want to understand why Earth can only rehearse parts of a mission. The welcome page offers a guided path for each.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Leaflet for the map, NASA GIBS map tiles, Python in Google Colab for data processing, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Light and dark themes, works on phones.
